title: Too Many Visitors?
intro: Tourism brings money and jobs to many places, but in some famous destinations people are starting to ask whether there can be too much of a good thing.

passage: Every summer, millions of people pack their bags and travel to the same famous places. In 1950, about 25 million international trips were made around the world. Today, the number is well over one billion each year. Cheap flights, online booking and social media have made travel easier than ever before, and a single beautiful photo can attract thousands of new visitors to a small town. But as more and more tourists arrive, many popular destinations are asking an important question: can a place have too many visitors?

For many countries, tourism is a vital source of income. Hotels, restaurants, guides and taxi drivers all depend on visitors, and in some small island nations, tourism makes up a large part of the whole economy. Money from tourism can also help to pay for new roads, airports and museums, which local people use as well. When tourists buy souvenirs from local craftspeople, the money goes directly to families who might otherwise struggle to find work.

However, the picture is not always so positive. In Venice, Italy, the number of residents in the historic centre has fallen to around 50,000, while millions of visitors walk through its narrow streets every year. Many people who live there say the city has become too crowded and too expensive. One reason is that landlords prefer to rent their flats to tourists, who pay more for a short stay. Similar complaints have been heard in Barcelona, Amsterdam and other European cities.

Mass tourism can also damage the natural world. Large cruise ships produce air and water pollution, and thousands of feet can wear away paths in mountains and forests. In 2018, Maya Bay in Thailand, which had become famous after it appeared in a Hollywood film, was closed to visitors because its coral and beach had been seriously damaged. The bay stayed closed for more than three years so that nature had time to recover.

Some places are now trying to find solutions. In 2024, Venice began to charge day visitors an entry fee on its busiest days. The small Himalayan country of Bhutan has asked tourists to pay a daily fee for many years, and this money is used to protect its environment and culture. Other cities limit the number of cruise ships that can stop there, or encourage tourists to come in quieter months, when hotels and streets are less busy.

Travellers themselves can help as well. Experts suggest choosing less famous destinations, staying longer in one place instead of rushing between cities, and spending money in small local businesses. Many people find that these trips feel more authentic, because they meet real people and see everyday life rather than long queues. If tourism is managed carefully, it can become sustainable, bringing benefits to visitors and to the people who call these places home.
